artworks.title: Daedalus and Icarus
artworks.description: Early van Dyck oil of the craftsman fastening wings to his son's shoulders: Daedalus, the labyrinth-builder exiled from Crete, prepares the flight that will free them from Minos and destroy the boy who flies too near the sun. The father's concentrated hands and Icarus' upward gaze fix the myth's fatal engineering.

artworks.title: Daedalus and Icarus
artworks.description: Baroque canvas by Andrea Sacchi in which Daedalus adjusts the wax-and-feather wings while Icarus looks skyward. Sacchi stages the Athenian inventor as both tender father and master artificer — the mind that built the labyrinth now building an escape from it.

artworks.title: Daedalus and Icarus
artworks.description: Attributed to Charles Le Brun: Daedalus binds the wings to Icarus against a luminous sky, the moment before their leap from Crete. French classicism turns the craftsman's caution into a moral tableau — skill and hubris paired in a single embrace.

artworks.title: Daedalus and Icarus
artworks.description: Caravaggesque oil by Orazio Riminaldi showing Daedalus fastening the wings to a youthful Icarus. Strong chiaroscuro isolates the craftsman's tools and touch — the inventor of the labyrinth rendered as an intimate scene of instruction before the fatal flight.

popCulture.title: The King Must Die
popCulture.creator: Mary Renault
popCulture.description: Renault's Crete is the craftsman's island: the labyrinth and the palace engineering that make Daedalus' name synonymous with cunning making.

popCulture.title: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
popCulture.creator: James Joyce
popCulture.description: Joyce names Stephen Dedalus after the labyrinth-builder — the artist who must craft wings to escape the nets of nation, language and religion.
